presentation, and restores process-duration display for segmented MCP
turns.

## User problem

External agents could ignore the injected `wanta_link` capability and
fall back to shell commands such as `oo connector run`. That produced
several user-visible failure modes during ordinary PostHog analysis:

- invalid CLI flags and shell quoting failures while the model assembled
JSON or HogQL;
- sandbox network failures followed by redundant permission escalation;
- behavior differences between OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code;
- successful reports accompanied by multiple alarming `Incomplete` tool
rows;
- provider credential fields reaching external-agent transcript storage
when a native path bypassed upstream redaction;
- missing process duration after Link calls moved to MCP tools without
native tool timing.

## Root cause

The host prompt described Wanta Link as the preferred transport, but the
local command permission policy still allowed raw connector business
commands. External agent subprocesses also did not all share the same
managed command environment. Transcript persistence assumed upstream
transports had already redacted sensitive fields. Finally, the process
timeline splits tool activity from the final response, so a process-only
segment could lose the enclosing turn's `completedAt` when MCP tool
parts had no timing data.

## Fix

- Add an agent-independent Link transport gate that rejects raw `oo
connector apps`, `run`, and `proxy` commands while a Wanta Link runtime
is active, including wrapped, piped, and redirected forms.
- Keep structured `inspect_action` and `call_action` as the required
business path and strengthen the host/Skill execution guidance.
- Give Claude Code and every ACP adapter the same Wanta-managed
subprocess environment and guarded `oo` fallback.
- Normalize invalid workspace selectors on identity-independent `schema`
and `search` compatibility calls.
- Add metadata-only capability-manifest and blocked-CLI diagnostics
without recording tool inputs, outputs, headers, or credentials.
- Add a final external transcript redaction boundary for live events,
in-memory history, persisted history, and legacy transcript migration,
including nested and escaped JSON credential fields.
- Add normalized native tool failure categories (`input`, `sandbox`,
`network`, `authorization`, `provider`, `agent_runtime`, and `unknown`)
with conservative user-impact classification.
- Present safe failed attempts as automatically handled when the turn
has a visible successful outcome, while preserving expandable error
details and unresolved failures.
- Inherit the enclosing turn timing envelope for the final process
segment so MCP-based turns retain duration display even when tool parts
do not carry native timing.

- `pnpm run ts-check`

`agent-comms-mcp-mint-token` (installed alongside the other console
scripts) mints agent-jwt Bearer tokens against `AGENT_JWT_SECRET`:

```bash
# Human-owned agent
agent-comms-mcp-mint-token --sub ea-agent-svc --scopes "comms:read comms:write" \

Fix real vulnerabilities found in a dedicated security audit

Three parallel audits (auth/authz, injection/input-handling, secrets/
infrastructure) covering the whole app, adversarial lens. Fixes:

CRITICAL
- MFA was completely bypassable: the 5-minute "mfa_pending" challenge
  token issued by /auth/login (before a TOTP/backup code is ever
  checked) decoded and passed get_current_user()'s checks exactly like
  a real session token -- anyone with just a password (the one thing
  MFA exists to add a second factor against) could call any
  authenticated endpoint directly with it, no code required, for the
  full 5-minute window. Now explicitly rejected, same pattern as the
  existing "purpose" claim check.

HIGH
- Twilio webhook signature verification failed OPEN (skipped, request
  allowed through) when TWILIO_TOKEN/PUBLIC_BASE_URL were unset --
  now fails closed (503), matching the pattern already used correctly
  for CRON_SECRET/EMAIL_WORKER_SECRET.
- SECRET_KEY/JWT_SECRET ship with hardcoded, publicly-known placeholder
  defaults with no code-level guard against running with them in
  production (only Render's generateValue: true prevented this on the
  documented deploy path). App now refuses to boot with DEBUG=false if
  either is still its literal default.

MODERATE
- Three IDOR gaps: POST /communications/send's maintenance_update
  template, POST /maintenance/'s unit_id/tenant_id, and POST
  /accounting/expenses' vendor_id all accepted a foreign org's UUID
  with no ownership check, leaking that resource's name/title/status
  back in the response. All now validated against the caller's org.
- Unescaped HTML injection in three outreach-email templates
  (services/lead_service.py) -- lead fields (scraped from public,
  attacker-editable Google Business Profile data, or typed into
  POST /leads with no sanitization) were interpolated into HTML emails
  with no output encoding. Now html.escape()'d for the HTML body
  specifically (plain-text body unaffected).
- SSRF in the lead-scraper's email-discovery fetch
  (workers/tasks/lead_scraping.py) -- a Places listing's self-reported
  website URL was fetched with no scheme/private-IP allowlist and
  followed redirects blindly, so a listing pointed at an internal
  address or a cloud metadata endpoint would have the server fetch it.
  Added an SSRF guard checked on the initial URL and re-checked on
  every redirect hop.
- FastAPI backend sent no security headers at all (X-Frame-Options,
  X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) --
  only the Next.js frontend did, despite security.tsx's copy claiming
  this applies to "every response." Left /docs and /redoc unprotected
  against framing. Added a headers middleware.
- ALLOWED_ORIGINS="*" combined with allow_credentials=True (a plausible
  operator typo in Render's env vars) would silently make CORS reflect
  any origin with credentials -- app now refuses to boot with that
  combination instead.
- Three endpoints doing real, billed AI/scraping work (inspection photo
  AI analysis, the Claude marketing-copy generator, the lead-scrape
  trigger) had zero rate limiting or cost cap beyond role/plan gating --
  a compromised privileged account or a buggy retry loop had no
  built-in ceiling on Anthropic/OpenAI/Google Places billing, and on
  this single-worker server a burst could also stall every other
  tenant's requests. Added reasonable per-minute limits to all three.

Not fixed here, flagged for a follow-up decision (both require either
a schema migration or a product/UX tradeoff, not a mechanical fix):
- Password reset tokens (staff-side /auth/reset-password) are replayable
  within their 30-minute window -- not marked single-use like the
  tenant-portal equivalent already is.
- Rate limiting on login/reset/2FA is per-IP only, no per-account
  lockout/backoff -- a distributed credential-stuffing attempt across
  many source IPs isn't meaningfully throttled today.
- API keys are stored and compared in plaintext (high-entropy,
  infeasible to brute-force, but a DB-level compromise would expose
  live keys directly rather than hashes) -- hashing at rest would need
  a rotation flow since existing keys can't be un-hashed.

* fix(patients): normalize patient phone to E.164 — fix public-booking OTP lockout

Patient phone numbers were stored in whatever format the operator typed
(bare 10-digit, 91…, +91…, with punctuation). Every caller that needed to
match a phone normalized the input first and then did an exact match —
which silently found nothing whenever the stored row was in a different
form. Public-booking's returning-patient OTP was the most visible victim:
findByClinicIdAndPhoneNumber always returned null, so requestOtp's
'if (patient)' guard never fired and no OTP was ever sent.

This fixes it on three layers, mirroring the portal fix already in prod:

1. Read-side tolerance — findByClinicIdAndPhoneNumber now does
   phoneNumber: { in: phoneMatchCandidates(phone) } so a row stored as
   '9812345678', '91…', or '+91…' all match an incoming '+91…' lookup.

2. Write-side normalization — PatientMapper normalizes the phone to E.164
   in both create and update paths, so all new writes land in a single
   canonical form regardless of what the caller passed.

3. Data migration — one-shot SQL rewrites existing bare-10-digit rows to
   '+91…'. Idempotent, skips soft-deleted rows, bumps version + updatedAt
   so any in-flight optimistic-concurrency update is rejected cleanly.

The normalize / matchCandidates helpers are extracted to
@workspace/utils (one source of truth for India-first phone handling) and
ported public-booking + patient-portal to use them. The pre-existing
private copy in prisma-portal-profile.repository is replaced.

three affected domains green; pnpm exec tsc --noEmit from apps/api is
clean; targeted ESLint clean. The migration is safe to defer — the
tolerant read-side lookup makes the OTP fix land without it.

## Development vs. evaluation

```text
corpus/
├── development/   public, tunable, regression-only — never a headline metric
└── evaluation/    the blind holdout — the only tier a headline metric can come from
```

This split exists for one reason: **the moment a fixture is used to diagnose
or fix a scanner bug, it stops measuring generalization and starts measuring
"did we regress on a known case."** Both are useful, but conflating them is
how a benchmark quietly turns into a training set its own maintainer is
unknowingly optimizing against.

The rule, mechanically enforced by `run_benchmark.py` (`validate_tier_matches_dir`)
and by policy for everything the tooling can't check automatically:

> **A fixture that has ever been used to diagnose, reproduce, or fix a
> scanner bug belongs in `development/` permanently. It must never move to
> `evaluation/`, regardless of how old the bug or how thoroughly it's since
> been fixed.**

The 12 fixtures this benchmark launched with already found two real skil
false positives (issues #33, #34) — which is exactly why all 12 are
classified `tier: development` and always will be, even after those issues
are fixed and the fixtures become permanent regression tests. `evaluation/`
starts empty. Filling it requires fixtures nobody has used to tune anything
against, which in practice means writing them somewhat independently of
active bug-fixing work, or asking someone who isn't fixing skil's bugs to
contribute them.

## Review status

Every fixture starts at `review.status: provisional`. A fixture only
becomes `gold` after **at least two independent human reviewers** agree
with its `ground_truth` and `rationale`. `run_benchmark.py` computes three
numbers per tool:

- **headline_metric** — `tier: evaluation` AND `review.status: gold` only.
  This is the only number meant to be quoted anywhere (README, `COMPARISON.md`,
  external claims). As of this benchmark's initial version, `evaluation/` is
  empty, so the headline metric correctly reads `"n/a"` for every tool.
  That's the runner working as designed, not a bug.
- **development_set_metric_regression_only_never_a_generalization_claim** —
  every `development/` fixture, regardless of review status. Use this to
  check for regressions after a fix; never cite it as evidence of detection
  quality.
- **evaluation_set_provisional_metric_informational_only** — `evaluation/`
  fixtures not yet at `gold`. Useful for iterating on new holdout fixtures
  before they're reviewed; also not a headline number.

fix(plaud-auth): stop the token refresh from destroying its own credentials

Plaud ingestion died 2026-08-17 and stayed dead for a day: chronos-pipeline
raised AuthenticationRequired every 6h because .plaud_tokens.json had been
deleted. Three separate defects in refresh_access_token() could each cause it.

1. Refresh sent an Authorization: Basic header. Plaud's published third-party
   spec sends the refresh request with only accept + content-type — Basic auth
   belongs on the code-exchange call, not this one. An unexpected Authorization
   header is a plausible source of the observed 401. Now tries the documented
   form first and falls back to the legacy Basic form, logging which the server
   accepted so the ambiguity resolves itself on the next real refresh.

2. Any HTTP error cleared the tokens. A 5xx, a 429 or a DNS blip would delete a
   valid refresh token and force a manual re-auth. Transient failures now retry
   three times with backoff and preserve the tokens; only a definitive 400/401
   clears them. Also adds a 30s timeout, which was missing entirely.

3. No concurrency control. chronos-api, chronos-auto-sync and chronos-pipeline
   each hold their own client against one shared token file, and Plaud rotates
   the refresh token on every refresh. One process rotates, another refreshes
   with the now-dead token, gets 401, and wipes the file. Refresh now holds an
   exclusive flock for the whole read-refresh-write cycle, re-reads the file
   after acquiring it, and on a 401 checks whether disk holds a newer token —
   adopting it instead of clearing.

Also makes deploy/watchdog.sh accept either https (self-signed) or http on
:8050, so the Dash UI switching protocol cannot trigger a restart loop.

Verified against mocked servers: rotation race keeps the file and the token;
genuine revocation still clears; transient 503/429/network preserve; and both
the spec and legacy header forms succeed.

bifrost added pre-shared-key authentication (nais/bifrost#549) and is
running in its accept phase: unauthenticated calls are allowed but logged
as "Request without a valid API key allowed (authentication not
enforced)". Every call nais-api makes is currently in that log.

Sends the key as "Authorization: Bearer <key>" on every bifrost request,
read from UNLEASH_BIFROST_API_KEY and provisioned through fasit to both
deployments.

An unset key sends no header at all rather than an empty one — a
present-but-empty credential is worse than none, since it looks like a
failed authentication rather than an unauthenticated caller. Startup logs
a warning in that case, because it is the state that breaks the moment
bifrost sets auth.enforced.

This is step 3 of nais/bifrost#576. It must be deployed and confirmed
before that flag is flipped; until then nothing changes behaviourally,
since bifrost accepts both.

Tests cover that the header is sent with the configured key and that no
header is sent without one; the first fails if the request editor is
removed.

* fix(unleash): actually deliver the bifrost key to the pod

The previous commit reads UNLEASH_BIFROST_API_KEY but nothing set it. The
chart wires UNLEASH_BIFROST_API_URL and no key, so the client would have
logged "No bifrost API key configured" and kept sending unauthenticated
requests — the rollout would have looked done while changing nothing.

Wires it end to end: the value is sourced from the fasit management value
bifrost_api_key, lands in the release Secret alongside the other
pre-shared keys, and reaches the container through the existing envFrom.

Same pattern as HOOKD_PSK and REST_PRE_SHARED_KEY, which is where a
secret belongs rather than a plain env value in the deployment.

* feat(chart): source the bifrost key from fasit

The key is computed from the management value. It is deliberately not
overridable per environment: staging the rollout is done with bifrost's
enforcement toggle, not by varying who holds the credential. One key,
one place it comes from.

parameter and internal/integration/manager.go was not updated. The

value, and bifrost accepts a comma-separated list so keys can be rotated
without downtime. nais-api sent the list verbatim, so a rotation value of

that shows up as unauthenticated_allowed; after it, a full outage at the
worst possible moment. The client now presents the first entry, so

Fix security findings from the August 2026 penetration tests

Cross-compared two Strix reports (timetify.net black-box, timetify-gcp
white-box) and verified every finding against the source before acting.

Confirmed and fixed:
- No rate limiting on auth endpoints (CRITICAL). Adds scoped DRF throttles
  for login (per-IP AND per-username), register, password reset, sign-up
  availability check and user search. Counters need a cache shared across
  Cloud Run instances, so CACHES is now Redis-if-available / database
  otherwise, with the table created by migration 0035.
- Public GCS bucket with unsigned URLs (HIGH). Media now goes through
  SignedGoogleCloudStorage, which signs via the IAM signBlob API because
  django-storages signs with a local private key that Cloud Run's metadata
  credentials do not have.
- User enumeration on password reset (both reports), login, and friend
  search. Constant response, generic auth error, 3-char search floor.
- Cross-tenant IDOR via writable `course` FK on Week/Exam/Assignment.
- Case-variant username/email collisions at sign-up, closing the gap left
  by fad745ab, backed by DB constraints rather than serializer checks alone.
- Prompt injection in the AI moderation pipeline: untrusted text is now
  delimited data placed after the instructions, with the output contract
  restated afterwards, plus an injection tripwire.
- Past-dated events, admin on a fixed path, missing CSP/HSTS/frame headers.

Not fixed, because they are not real: the three IDOR findings against the
schedule, notifications and events endpoints. All three views derive the
user from request.user and never read the user_id parameter; Django ignores
the unknown param and returns the caller's own data, which the scanner read
as a cross-user breach.

Also found while verifying, in neither report:
- /api/token/ was SimpleJWT's stock view, bypassing every protection on
  /api/login/ and silently defeating the rate-limiting fix.
- Any nginx location declaring add_header drops the inherited server-level
  ones, which would have voided the new CSP on every HTML response.
- CourseSerializer.parent_course had the same unvalidated-FK hole.
- Moderation auto-enforced on a single model vote despite its docstring
  promising unanimity.
- Password reset matched email case-sensitively.

gunicorn, python-dotenv and pg8000. pip-audit and check --deploy both clean.

Adds 23 regression tests; full suite 162 passing.
